chunks.content: Introduction Gastric cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with Japan exhibiting the highest age-standardized incidence [ ]. Among patients with advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, ~20% exhibit overexpression of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), which defines a biologically and clinically distinct subgroup requiring tailored therapeutic strategies [ , ]. For HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer (AGC), international guidelines such as the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) and European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) recommend trastuzumab-based therapy in the first-line setting and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in subsequent lines [ , ]. In Japan, following the results of the DESTINY-Gastric01 trial [ ], T-DXd received approval in September 2020 and has since been incorporated as a third-line recommendation in the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association (JGCA) 2021 guidelines [ ]. Before T-DXd became available, nivolumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI), was the most commonly prescribed drug as third- or later-line treatment in patients with HER2-positive AGC in Japan [ ]. Emerging evidence has suggested that HER2-positive tumors may exhibit an immunologically active microenvironment, including increased programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, and that prior ICI exposure may potentiate the effects of subsequent therapies [ ]. Preclinical studies have shown that HER2 signaling plays a role in regulating the recruitment and activation of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, and anti–programmed death protein (PD)-1 antibodies could significantly increase the therapeutic activity of HER2 inhibitors [ , ]. Iwata et al. reported that combination therapy with T-DXd and ICI resulted in enhanced antitumor immunity compared with that observed with either monotherapy [ ]. Furthermore, Osa et al. also reported that nivolumab showed controlled levels of lymphocyte-surface PD-1–blocking activity for more than 2 months [ ]. Although the DESTINY-Gastric01 trial included some patients with prior ICI exposure and showed numerically better outcomes in this subgroup, the impact of ICI–T-DXd sequencing and timing has not been fully characterized in the real-world setting [ ]. The EN-DEAVOR study, a nationwide retrospective observational cohort study in Japan, previously confirmed the effectiveness and safety of T-DXd in routine clinical practice [ ]. While previous analyses within this study reported no differences in overall survival (OS) and real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) based on prior ICI therapy, a comprehensive evaluation of the sequencing and timing between ICI and T-DXd therapies has not yet been performed [ , ]. In this exploratory analysis of EN-DEAVOR, we explored whether the timing of T-DXd administration in relation to prior nivolumab therapy affects clinical outcomes. We compared effectiveness and safety across subgroups stratified by the interval between the last dose of nivolumab and the first dose of T-DXd. This analysis provides real-world evidence regarding the potential synergy of subsequent T-DXd therapy in patients who previously received ICI-containing regimens. Patients and methods Study design This exploratory post hoc subgroup analysis was conducted using the EN-DEAVOR data set. EN-DEAVOR was a retrospective, observational, real-world cohort study conducted across 63 sites in Japan between 25 September 2020 and 30 September 2021 (UMIN000049032) [ ]. The study was approved by the institutional ethical review board of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine (No. 2022–0170). All patients provided written informed consent to participate in this study. However, opt-out registration was allowed for patients when obtaining written informed consent was challenging due to various reasons. Eligibility criteria and subgroups Patients aged ≥20 years with a histopathologically confirmed diagnosis of HER2-positive (immunohistochemistry [IHC] 3+ or IHC 2+ with in situ hybridization [ISH]+) unresectable advanced or recurrent gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma that had worsened after chemotherapy and who had started treatment with T-DXd were included in the primary analysis [ ]. This post hoc analysis examined the following patient subgroups: (i) those who received their first dose of T-DXd treatment within 2 months after the final dose of nivolumab (Group A), (ii) those who received their first dose of T-DXd treatment more than 2 months after the final dose of nivolumab (Group B), and (iii) those who did not receive nivolumab prior to T-DXd treatment (Group C). The cutoff of 2 months was selected based on the findings by Osa et al [ ]. Study endpoints The primary effectiveness endpoints included rwPFS across the three patient subgroups, as well as objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and best overall response (BOR) in patients presenting with target lesions. Exploratory endpoints included median OS and relative OS and relative rwPFS based on different time intervals between the first dose of T-DXd administration and the final dose of nivolumab treatment (i.e. ≤2/>2 months, ≤3/>3 months, ≤4/>4 months, and ≤5/>5 months). The exploratory analysis also included types of treatments administered to participants after T-DXd. The safety endpoint included the incidence of grade ≥ 3 adverse events (AEs) in the three patient subgroups. Statistical analysis The sample size was set to 300 patients

objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), and best overall response (BOR) in patients presenting with target lesions. Exploratory endpoints included median OS and relative OS and relative rwPFS based on different time intervals between the first dose of T-DXd administration and the final dose of nivolumab treatment (i.e. ≤2/>2 months, ≤3/>3 months, ≤4/>4 months, and ≤5/>5 months). The exploratory analysis also included types of treatments administered to participants after T-DXd. The safety endpoint included the incidence of grade ≥ 3 adverse events (AEs) in the three patient subgroups. Statistical analysis The sample size was set to 300 patients considering the data collection feasibility at the participating study sites. The analysis population comprised all patients registered for the study, except those with significant protocol deviations and those deemed ineligible at the case-review meeting. For the univariable and multivariable analyses, P values were calculated for the Cox proportional hazards model and the logistic regression model. The significance level for hypothesis testing was 5% two-sided. No extra complementing process was conducted if missing data were detected. Data are presented as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence interval (CI) for rwPFS and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS software version 9.4. Results Patient disposition Of 312 patients enrolled in the primary analysis, 63 were in Group A, 63 were in Group B, and 185 were in Group C. One patient with missing data on the duration or timing of nivolumab administration was excluded from the analysis. Demographics and baseline clinical characteristics Baseline patient characteristics were generally well balanced between the three groups ( ). The mean (standard deviation) age was 67.3 (9.5), 68.1 (10.3), and 67.5 (11.3) years in Groups A, B, and C, respectively. Majority of the patients across all groups were male; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status score of 0 or 1; and presented with primary lesions in the stomach, metastases in two or more organs, and with the lymph nodes as the primary site of metastasis. Group B predominantly consisted of patients (84.1%) who had undergone a higher number of prior lines of therapy (≥4). However, 66.7% of patients in Group A had received 3 prior lines of therapy, while 83.8% of patients in Group C had undergone only 1–2 prior lines of therapy, with the difference being statistically significant ( P < .0001). Primary effectiveness endpoints The median (95% CI) rwPFS (months) was 6.93 (4.57–7.79), 4.63 (3.75–5.75), and 4.17 (3.71–4.76) in Groups A, B, and C, respectively ( ). The risk of progression was significantly lower in Group A compared with Group B (HR [95% CI]: 0.59 [0.40–0.87]; P = .0074; ). The ORR was numerically higher in Group A at 54.9% (95% CI: 40.3–68.9) compared with Group B at 30.8% (95% CI: 18.7–45.1; ). The DCR was comparable across groups: 80.4% (95% CI: 66.9–90.2) in Group A, 82.7% (95% CI: 69.7–91.8) in Group B, and 82.0% (95% CI: 74.0–88.3) in Group C ( ). The BOR demonstrated varying outcomes among the three groups. Partial response (PR) was most notable in Group A, where 51.0% of patients achieved a tumor reduction, compared with 28.8% in Group B and 41.8% in Group C. Stable disease (SD) was observed most frequently in Group B, with 51.9% of patients showing no disease progression, compared with 25.5% and 38.5% in Groups A and C, respectively ( ). Exploratory endpoints The median (95% CI) OS (months) was 11.56 (7.03–13.50), 8.15 (6.83–9.00), and 9.89 (7.46–11.83) in Groups A, B, and C, respectively ( ). The survival rate was numerically higher in Group A compared with Group B (HR [95% CI]: 0.79 [0.53–1.17]; P = .2397; ). Overall, there was a slight trend that survival rate was higher in patients who received T-DXd treatment ≤2/>2 months after nivolumab therapy (HR [95% CI]: 0.79 [0.53–1.17]) compared with those who received T-DXd treatment ≤3/>3 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.87 [0.58–1.30]), ≤4/>4 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.97 [0.65–1.46]), and ≤5/>5 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.93 [0.62–1.40]) after nivolumab therapy ( ). Overall, risk of progression was lower in patients who received T-DXd treatment ≤2/>2 months after nivolumab therapy (HR [95% CI]: 0.59 [0.40–0.87]) compared with those who received T-DXd treatment ≤3/>3 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.67 [0.45–0.98]), ≤4/>4 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.70 [0.47–1.03]), and ≤5/>5 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.74 [0.50–1.09]) after nivolumab therapy ( ). The treatment rates post–T-DXd therapy were 54.0%, 47.6%, and 70.3% in Groups A, B, and C, respectively ( ). Large proportions of patients in all the groups received chemotherapy (Group A: 50.8%; Group B: 39.7%; Group C: 65.9%). Multivariate analysis incorporating the interval between completion of prior nivolumab therapy and initiation of T-DXd showed that patients who received T-DXd within a shorter interval after nivolumab completion experienced significantly improved rwPFS outcomes (HR [95% CI]: 0.63 [0.44–0.89]; P

CI]: 0.67 [0.45–0.98]), ≤4/>4 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.70 [0.47–1.03]), and ≤5/>5 months (HR [95% CI]: 0.74 [0.50–1.09]) after nivolumab therapy ( ). The treatment rates post–T-DXd therapy were 54.0%, 47.6%, and 70.3% in Groups A, B, and C, respectively ( ). Large proportions of patients in all the groups received chemotherapy (Group A: 50.8%; Group B: 39.7%; Group C: 65.9%). Multivariate analysis incorporating the interval between completion of prior nivolumab therapy and initiation of T-DXd showed that patients who received T-DXd within a shorter interval after nivolumab completion experienced significantly improved rwPFS outcomes (HR [95% CI]: 0.63 [0.44–0.89]; P = .0081; ). No significant differences were observed for OS or ORR ( & ). Safety endpoints The incidence rate of grade ≥ 3 AEs was stratified by duration of prior trastuzumab treatment ( ). More patients in Group B (58.7%) experienced grade ≥ 3 AEs than in Group A (50.8%) and Group C (43.8%). In Group A, hematotoxicity was observed in 25.4% of patients, with neutrophil count reduction being the most common hematologic event (22.2%). In Group B, hematotoxicity was more prominent, affecting 42.9% of patients, with anemia being the most frequent hematologic AE (27.0%). Decreased neutrophil count and anorexia occurred in 19.0% and 7.9% of patients, respectively. The incidence of interstitial pneumonia was 6.3% in both Groups A and B and 3.2% in Group C. Discussion The previous EN-DEAVOR study assessing the real-world effectiveness of T-DXd in Japanese patients with HER2+ AGC showed no difference in efficacy regardless of prior ICI therapy, such as with nivolumab, indicating that nivolumab administration was not a prognostic factor for OS [ ] or rwPFS [ ]. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-world report to examine the detailed impact of timing between prior ICI therapy and subsequent T-DXd treatment in patients with HER2-positive AGC. This exploratory analysis of EN-DEAVOR demonstrated that initiating T-DXd within 2 months following the final dose of nivolumab was associated with significantly improved rwPFS and numerically higher ORR, compared to delayed administration. These benefits were achieved without an increase in grade ≥ 3 AEs, supporting the feasibility of this sequencing strategy in clinical practice. One plausible explanation for the favorable rwPFS in patients who started T-DXd earlier is the persistence of immune modulation induced by prior nivolumab therapy [ ]. Sustained PD-1 receptor occupancy, as demonstrated by Osa et al., may maintain an activated immune milieu during the initial phase of T-DXd treatment [ ]. Given that HER2 signaling has been implicated in modulating immune cell dynamics within the tumor microenvironment, T-DXd may exert greater efficacy when administered in this preconditioned immunologic setting [ ]. The interplay between these mechanisms suggests that treatment sequencing could be a key determinant of therapeutic success. The findings of this study align with previous exploratory analyses of the DESTINY-Gastric-01 trial focusing on the effects of ICI, suggesting that prior immunotherapy might increase the efficacy of subsequent treatment with T-DXd [ ]. Moreover, the REVIVE real-world study suggested enhanced effectiveness of chemotherapy following ICI, further supporting the hypothesis that recent immunotherapy may sensitize tumors to subsequent systemic treatments [ ]. Our results extend these observations to a large real-world cohort and provide additional evidence that close sequencing of ICI and T-DXd may confer clinical benefit. Interestingly, while rwPFS was significantly prolonged in Group A, no statistically significant difference in OS was observed between groups. Although the baseline characteristics were mostly comparable between the study groups, the majority of patients in Group A (66.7%) and Group B (84.1%) received T-DXd after 3 and ≥4 prior lines of therapy, respectively. The difference in the number of lines of therapy in each group needs to be considered carefully. Although the DESTINY-Gastric-01 trial suggested comparable T-DXd efficacy regardless of the number of prior lines of therapy, the potential impact on OS in more heavily pretreated populations remains uncertain [ ]. However, no data were available regarding its impact on rwPFS. Therefore, while OS remains a clinically meaningful endpoint, it may be more susceptible to variability in treatment patterns and patient characteristics in non-randomized, observational cohorts, and should be interpreted in this setting. From a safety perspective, the incidence of grade ≥ 3 AEs was comparable across subgroups, and no new safety signals were identified. The slightly higher hematologic toxicity observed in Group B may be attributable to more intensive prior treatment history. Notably, interstitial lung disease, a known risk of both nivolumab and T-DXd, occurred at a relatively low rate and did not appear to be exacerbated by close sequencing of the two agents [ , ]. This supports the clinical feasibility of administering T-DXd shortly after ICI, although careful monitoring remains essential. This study has several clinical implications. The slightly higher hematologic toxicity observed in Group B may be attributable to more intensive prior treatment history. Notably, interstitial lung disease, a known risk of both nivolumab and T-DXd, occurred at a relatively low rate and did not appear to be exacerbated by close sequencing of the two agents [ , ]. This supports the clinical feasibility of administering T-DXd shortly after ICI, although careful monitoring remains essential. This study has several clinical implications. As ICIs are increasingly used in earlier lines of therapy, including as part of first-line regimens for HER2-positive AGC, our findings suggest that initiating T-DXd soon after ICI cessation may leverage the residual immunologic effects of PD-1 blockade and improve treatment outcomes. These insights may be particularly valuable in treatment settings where T-DXd is approved for second-line use and may inform the design of future sequencing strategies in HER2-positive AGC. Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, this was a retrospective, post hoc analysis of an observational cohort, and treatment assignment was not randomized. Second, the small number of patients or the prior use of ICI therapy may have led to imbalances in key baseline characteristics, such as the number of prior lines of therapy, which can impact clinical outcomes, and the results should be interpreted with caution as T-DXd was administered immediately after prior ICI (within 2 months) more commonly in patients who had received 3 lines of therapy compared with patients who had received 4 lines of therapy. Although both ICI and T-DXd can be administered as third-line monotherapy, as stated in the Japanese guidelines [ ], the treatment sequence of ICI after T-DXd has not been investigated in this study; therefore, it is not possible to ascertain whether there would be differences in treatment outcome based on treatment sequence and which treatment sequence should be followed. Third, PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) data were not consistently available in this cohort. As CPS may influence ICI response and treatment selection, especially in the first-line setting for HER2-positive AGC, its absence limits interpretation of immunologic context and may represent a potential confounder. Finally, assessment of therapeutic effects was based on data collected in real-world clinical practice and was not based on standardized criteria. Validation of these results using a prospective clinical trial approach is needed. Conclusion T-DXd was effective regardless of prior ICI treatment, but the timing of its initiation following ICI therapy appears to influence treatment outcomes. This study showed the effectiveness of T-DXd across subgroups, with optimal outcomes when initiated promptly after nivolumab therapy. Given the evolving treatment landscape for gastric cancer, including the increasing use of ICI agents in first-line therapy, the results of this study may support clinicians in determining the optimal sequencing of therapies to provide best possible outcomes for patients with AGC. Introduction Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) are rare sarcomas arising from Cajal's interstitial cells across the entire gastrointestinal (GI) tract, representing approximately 0.1%-3% of all GI malignancies. , More than 85% of patients with GIST harbour an oncogenic KIT (∼75% of cases) or platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA, ∼10% of cases) mutation that drives tumour growth. For localised, potentially resectable disease, initial treatment includes surgery followed by adjuvant therapy with imatinib for patients with increased risk of recurrence (i.e. high mitotic index or large tumour size). Since non-targeted chemotherapy and radiation are largely ineffective, the current recommendation for advanced GIST involves the sequential administration of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib. , First-line treatment with imatinib is associated with a 60% response rate and median progression-free survival (PFS) of 18-24 months. Subsequent treatment with sunitinib and regorafenib achieve response rates of 5%-7%, and a median PFS of 5-6 months. Avapritinib (AYVAKYT®) is a type 1 TKI designed to inhibit both KIT and PDGFRA mutants, including activation loop mutants that escape approved therapies. , , Avapritinib showed marked selectivity for KIT and PDGFRA in a comprehensive kinome screening. The medicinal product was designated as an orphan medicinal product on 17 July 2017 for the treatment of GIST. To qualify for orphan designation, a medicine must be intended for the treatment, prevention, or diagnosis of a life-threatening or chronically debilitating disease, the prevalence of the condition in the European Union (EU) must not be >5 in 10 000, and the medicine must be of significant benefit to those affected by the condition. The final indication approved by the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) was ‘avapritinib is indicated as monotherapy for the treatment of adult patients with unresectable or metastatic GIST harbouring the PDGFRA D842V mutation.’ The review was conducted by CHMP and a positive opinion was issued on 23 July 2020. Nonclinical aspects and clinical pharmacology Avapritinib showed broad inhibitory activity against a panel of GIST relevant KIT and PDGFRA mutant enzymes, including the KIT exon 11, 17 and 18 mutants, and all PDGFRA exon 18 mutants tested. In contrast, the medicinal product demonstrated a lower binding affinity for wild-type KIT, wild-type PDGFRA, PDGFRB, CSF1R and FLT3. In vivo studies showed significant activity in several tumour models harbouring KIT mutations, with inhibition of KIT mutant activity and downstream signalling markers. Although inhibition of PDGFRA exon 18 mutants was demonstrated, the effect of avapritinib in PDGFRA-driven in vivo tumour models was not examined. Avapritinib is a CYP3A substrate, and concomitant use of strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors should be avoided. Based on in vitro data, avapritinib has been shown to autoinhibit and induce CYP3A enzymes. Population pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis indicated that age, race, sex, body weight, albumin concentration, mild hepatic impairment, or mild or moderate renal impairment had no clinically meaningful effect on the PK of avapritinib. Avapritinib had a large interpatient PK variability, with an 8- to 10-fold range in exposure at the 300 mg dose level. Across this exposure range, there was no apparent exposure-efficacy relationship. By contrast, relationships were observed between increasing avapritinib exposure and safety endpoints such as cognitive effects, increased bilirubin and decreased haemoglobin. A relationship was also observed between steady-state exposure at day 15 and time to dose interruption or reduction. All patients within the lowest quartile of exposure withstood the 300 mg dose for 2 months, while patients in the 2nd to 4th quartile required dose reductions after 1 month. Still, the currently approved dosing strategy is starting all patients with the 300 mg dose and lowering the dose in reaction to occurring adverse effects. Trial design A single pivotal study (BLU-285-1101, NAVIGATOR study) was presented to support the claimed indication. , This was a phase I, first-in-human, dose-escalation, open-label study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, PK, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy of avapritinib in adults with unresectable GIST. The population included in the initial proposed indication was composed by two different patient subsets: (i) patients with GIST who had received at least three lines of prior therapy (4L+ population, n = 121); and (ii) patients with GIST carrying the PDGFRA D842V mutation, regardless of number of prior therapies ( n = 38). The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR), defined as the rate of centrally confirmed complete or partial response by modified RECIST (mRECIST) (version 1.1). Key secondary endpoints were duration of response (DOR), PFS, and clinical benefit rate as per mRECIST version 1.1. Overall survival (OS) was included as an exploratory efficacy endpoint. Supportive studies were BLU-285-1303 and BLU-285-1105. BLU-285-1303 (VOYAGER) was a global, open-label, randomised, phase III trial designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of avapritinib versus regorafenib in patients with GIST who had received two or more lines of therapy. Patients were randomised (1 : 1)

38). The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR), defined as the rate of centrally confirmed complete or partial response by modified RECIST (mRECIST) (version 1.1). Key secondary endpoints were duration of response (DOR), PFS, and clinical benefit rate as per mRECIST version 1.1. Overall survival (OS) was included as an exploratory efficacy endpoint. Supportive studies were BLU-285-1303 and BLU-285-1105. BLU-285-1303 (VOYAGER) was a global, open-label, randomised, phase III trial designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of avapritinib versus regorafenib in patients with GIST who had received two or more lines of therapy. Patients were randomised (1 : 1) to receive either avapritinib (300 mg daily dose) or regorafenib (160 mg daily dose for 3 weeks followed by 1 week off medication). The primary endpoint was PFS by blinded, independent central radiology review, based on mRECIST version 1.1 criteria. BLU-285-1105 was an open-label, multicentre, phase I/II study designed to evaluate the safety, PK and clinical efficacy of avapritinib in Chinese patients with unresectable or metastatic GIST. In all trials, avapritinib was administered in continuous 28-day courses until unacceptable toxicity or progressive disease. Mutational PDGFRA D842V status was centrally assessed. During the evaluation, the applicant withdrew the fourth-line indication request from the marketing authorisation application. Clinical efficacy The dose finding phase was conducted following a 3 + 3 design in which dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) were assessed in continuous 28-day courses. The optimal biologically active dose was unknown, and the maximum tolerated dose was initially set to 400 mg daily due to DLT observed at the 600 mg daily dose. After initiation of the study extension, the starting dose was reduced to 300 mg daily in view of common treatment interruptions and dose reductions due to adverse events (AEs). The number of patients with unresectable or metastatic PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST who received 300 or 400 mg daily recruited into the BLU-285-1101 (NAVIGATOR) trial was 38. The regulatory decision was based on results from the cut-off date (COD) of 17 April 2020 (median follow-up of 26 months). In this patient population, 36/38 (95%) responses were observed [95% confidence interval (CI) 82.3% to 99.4%], including 5 (13%) complete responses, with a median DOR of 22.1 months [95% CI 14.1-not estimable (NE) months, ] and a median PFS of 24 months (95% CI 18.4-NE months). At the same COD, the median OS had not been reached yet, but the estimated OS at 36 months was 70.6% (95% CI 55.2-86.0 months) ( ). In the BLU-285-1303 (VOYAGER) study, at the COD of 9 March 2020, the ORR were 42.9% (all partial responses) versus 0% in the subset of patients with PDGFRA D842V mutations receiving avapritinib ( n = 7) versus regorafenib ( n = 6), respectively. The median PFS was not estimable (95% CI 9.7-NE months) versus 4.5 months (95% CI 1.7-NE months) for patients receiving avapritinib and regorafenib, respectively. Results from study BLU-285-1105, although limited ( n = 8), are considered supportive of the benefit–risk of avapritinib in the target patient population: five patients achieved a partial response (62.5% ORR) and three had stable disease. Clinical safety The safety profile of avapritinib was characterised in 585 patients with GIST (all doses), of whom 550 received avapritinib at a starting dose of 300 or 400 mg, including 250 patients from BLU-285-1101 and 335 patients from BLU-285-1303 (239 initially allocated to avapritinib and 96 initially allocated to regorafenib but crossed over to avapritinib due to disease progression) ( ). The median relative dose intensity was 90%, and the median treatment duration was 23.2 months for patients included in the BLU-285-1101 study and 8.9 months for patients included in the BLU-285-1303 study. An updated safety database with a COD of 9 March 2020 was submitted during the procedure. Safety data from BLU-285-1101 showed that all patients except one (>99%) reported at least one AE, where 80% had grade ≥3 AEs (13% fatal), 65% had serious AEs (SAEs), and 27% had events that led to permanent drug discontinuation. The most common fatal AEs were disease progression (15/32), physical deterioration (6/32), sepsis (3/32), and tumour haemorrhage (2/32). Cognitive AEs were reported by 46% (115/250) of the patients (90% grade 1-2 and 10% grade 3), with a median time to onset of 8.3 weeks. Of note, the median treatment duration was 12.4 months in patients who experienced cognitive AEs and 3.8 months in those patients who did not. The most common cognitive AEs were memory impairment, followed by cognitive disorders, confusional state, and encephalopathy. Intracranial haemorrhage was reported in 3% (7/250) of patients. No fatal cognitive or intracranial bleeding AEs were reported. The safety data in the subset of 56 patients with GIST and PDGFRA D842V mutations were consistent with the overall study population: 100% experienced AEs (80% ≥grade 3), 57% experienced SAEs, and 21% experienced AEs leading to permanent

onset of 8.3 weeks. Of note, the median treatment duration was 12.4 months in patients who experienced cognitive AEs and 3.8 months in those patients who did not. The most common cognitive AEs were memory impairment, followed by cognitive disorders, confusional state, and encephalopathy. Intracranial haemorrhage was reported in 3% (7/250) of patients. No fatal cognitive or intracranial bleeding AEs were reported. The safety data in the subset of 56 patients with GIST and PDGFRA D842V mutations were consistent with the overall study population: 100% experienced AEs (80% ≥grade 3), 57% experienced SAEs, and 21% experienced AEs leading to permanent treatment discontinuation. The safety analysis from the ongoing BLU-285-1303 study was also consistent with the results reported in the BLU-285-1101 study. Based on the pooled analysis of studies BLU-285-1101 and BLU-285-1303, the most frequently reported treatment-related AEs were nausea (45%), fatigue (40%), anaemia (39%), periorbital oedema (33%), hyperbilirubinaemia (27%), face oedema (27%), diarrhoea (26%), vomiting (24%), increased bilirubin (24%), peripheral oedema (23%), increased lacrimation (22%), decreased appetite (21%) and memory impairment (20%). The most common SAEs were anaemia (6%) and pleural effusion (1%), whereas the most common AEs leading to permanent treatment discontinuation were fatigue, encephalopathy and intracranial haemorrhage. Benefit–risk assessment The efficacy of avapritinib was evaluated in 59 patients with GIST harbouring a PDGFRA D842V mutation from the NAVIGATOR, VOYAGER, and BLU-285-1105 studies. The pivotal evidence supporting the indication comes from a small population ( n = 38) selected from the single-arm NAVIGATOR study that used ORR as a primary endpoint. The results were, however, unprecedented with a 95% ORR and a median DOR of 22.1 months. Data on TKI-naive patients appeared consistent with those of the overall PDGFRA D842V-mutant group, but were even more limited ( n = 5). However, it was agreed that results would not be expected to be of a lesser magnitude in the first-line setting and the benefit was considered demonstrated regardless of the line of treatment. Supportive data from the phase III, controlled study and the phase I study in Chinese patients also showed favourable and clinically relevant results, although of smaller magnitude. Overall, the reported results are considered clinically meaningful in the context of a patient population with limited treatment options and poor response to approved TKI agents. The safety database was substantially extended throughout the assessment procedure, with a median treatment duration of 23.2 months in the BLU-285-1101 study and 8.9 months in the BLU-285-1303 study. The safety profile was largely consistent with that reported for other TKIs. Intracranial bleeding and GI/tumour haemorrhage have been reported and remain AEs of concern. Cognitive disorders were very frequently reported, ranging from common occurrences of mild memory impairment events to rare cases of severe encephalopathy. Both intracranial haemorrhage and cognitive effects were identified as important risks in the risk management plan, including recommendations for dose modification in case of grade 1-3 events and permanent discontinuation in case of grade 4 events. Updated data revealed that the frequency of fatal AEs, SAEs, and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation were lower compared with those reported in the phase I study, and like those observed in the regorafenib control arm. Also, less cognitive AEs and episodes of intracranial bleeding were reported in the phase III trial. Overall, toxicity was manageable with appropriate risk minimisation measures, including close monitoring of AEs. Finally, longer-term follow-up is still needed as uncertainties remain on the safety profile of avapritinib, particularly in patients treated in the first-line setting. As comprehensive clinical data on the safety and efficacy of avapritinib were not available, a conditional marketing authorisation (CMA) was requested by the applicant in the initial submission. The following requirements were met: • Positive risk–benefit ratio: The applicant presented high and durable tumour responses that were unprecedented in this patient population with a manageable safety profile. • Likelihood that comprehensive clinical data will be provided: Specific obligations were imposed by CHMP. Final clinical study reports from studies BLU-285-1101 and BLU-285-1303 will include all available data on the safety and efficacy of avapritinib in patients with PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST ( n = 51). A new study (BLU-285-1406) will contribute with long-term (minimum 2 years) safety and efficacy data in approximately 50 previously untreated patients with GIST harbouring the PDGFRA D842V mutation. Overall, the proposed studies will contribute comprehensive clinical data in approximately 100 patients with PDGFRA D842V-mutant GIST. • Unmet medical need: The activity of currently available drugs is almost negligible in GIST patients with the PDGFRA D842V mutation. • The benefit to public health of immediate availability outweighs the risk that additional data are still required: The outstanding activity in a population with an unmet medical need renders the limited evidence acceptable for grant approval. As a result, CHMP decided to grant a CMA to avapritinib ‘as monotherapy for the treatment of adult

with GIST harbouring the PDGFRA D842V mutation. chunks.content: Introduction Colorectal cancer (CRC) stands as one of the most prevalent malignancies globally and the second leading cause of cancer-related death, presenting significant challenges despite advancements in diagnosis and treatment. , Among CRC patients, those at stage II represent a diverse cohort characterized by a lack of metastatic spread or lymph node involvement, with the main treatment being surgical resection of the primary tumor. While surgical resection is curative for most patients, approximately 15–20% of stage II CRC patients experience disease recurrence within five years, − with most recurrences detected before the first two years after diagnosis. This CRC recurrence is primarily due to undetected micrometastases or molecular abnormalities that elude conventional diagnostic approaches. The role of adjuvant chemotherapy in stage II disease is debated, and adjuvant treatment decisions are often based on risk assessment using traditional clinicopathologic characteristic. The heterogeneity of stage II CRC outcomes underscores the importance of identifying patients at higher risk for recurrence, as prognosis drastically worsens in these cases compared to nonrecurrent counterparts. , , , Five-year survival rates for nonrecurrent stage II CRC exceed 80%, while recurrent cases frequently develop distant metastases or locoregional recurrences, significantly reducing survival rates. − Major prognostic parameters defining high-risk stage II CRC include inadequate lymph node sampling (<12 nodes) and pT4 stage, while minor prognostic parameters comprise high-grade histology, vascular or lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, tumor obstruction, and elevated preoperative CEA levels. − Additionally, tumor budding has been recently further emphasized as an additional histopathological feature associated with recurrence risk. Notably, KRAS mutations are not considered a poor prognostic factor in stage II CRC, and microsatellite instability (MSI-high) represents a favorable prognostic marker that typically excludes adjuvant chemotherapy. − Despite these recently established clinicopathological indicators, current risk models still lack the precision required to reliably predict recurrence in stage II CRC, underscoring the need for novel molecular and proteomic tools capable of improving patient stratification and therapeutic decision-making. Recent advances in molecular biology and proteomics have revealed the potential of novel biomarkers in improving CRC management. − Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples, a staple in histopathology, are increasingly utilized in biomarker research due to their abundance and retrospective diagnostic potential. , Complementing this, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), particularly exosomes, have emerged as critical mediators of intercellular communication and promising sources of tumor-derived molecular data. , sEVs, which encapsulate proteins, RNA, and DNA, can be isolated from blood and other biological fluids, , offering a minimally invasive means to detect and monitor molecular changes reflective of the tumor microenvironment associated with CRC progression and recurrence. In this context, we performed here the proteomic profiling of paired FFPE tissues and plasma sEVs with the aim of identifying specific alterations linked to tumor aggressiveness and recurrence in stage II CRC patients, making findings of interest for both diagnostic and prognostic applications. Beyond recurrence, these biomarkers, after validation by WB, ELISA, immunohistochemistry, functional cell-based assays, and in silico analysis using tissue biopsies and plasma from CRC patients and controls, may serve as prognostic markers (i.e., MANF) and/or targets of intervention, opening avenues for personalized interventions aimed at mitigating recurrences and metastasis and improving survival outcomes. Materials and Methods Human Samples The Institutional Ethical Review Boards of the Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Hospital Clnico San Carlos (Madrid, Spain), and Hospital La Paz (IdiPAZ, Madrid, Spain), which belong to the National Biobank Network (ISCIII) cofounded with FEDER funds, approved this study on biomarker discovery and validation (CEI PI 13, CEI PI 13_2020-v2, and CEI PI 49). Paired plasma and FFPE tissue samples from CRC patients at stage II with recurrent and nonrecurrent CRC were obtained from La Paz Hospital using a standardized sample collection protocol, histopathologically analyzed, and stored at 4 °C until use. − Paired tumoral and nontumoral optimal cutting temperature (OCT)-embedded frozen tissue samples were obtained from the Hospital Clnico San Carlos (IdISSC) biobank after approval of the Ethical Review Boards of these institutions. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. Tissue samples were collected using a standardized sample collection protocol and stored at −80 °C until use. For mass spectrometry analysis, patients with microsatellite-stable stage II CRC and complete surgical resection (R0) were included in the study. All patients had a minimum clinical follow-up of three years, unless death due to disease occurred earlier. Therefore, FFPE tissue samples obtained by macrodissection from CRC patients at stage II with recurrent ( n = 5) and nonrecurrent ( n = 5) CRC were used ( ; Table S1 ). Additionally, sEVs were isolated from plasma samples from the same stage II CRC patients. For WB analysis, paired healthy and tumoral OCT-embedded frozen tissue samples from seven CRC patients at stages I ( n = 2), II ( n = 2), III ( n = 2), and IV ( n = 1)

had a minimum clinical follow-up of three years, unless death due to disease occurred earlier. Therefore, FFPE tissue samples obtained by macrodissection from CRC patients at stage II with recurrent ( n = 5) and nonrecurrent ( n = 5) CRC were used ( ; Table S1 ). Additionally, sEVs were isolated from plasma samples from the same stage II CRC patients. For WB analysis, paired healthy and tumoral OCT-embedded frozen tissue samples from seven CRC patients at stages I ( n = 2), II ( n = 2), III ( n = 2), and IV ( n = 1) were used ( ; Table S1 ). Plasma samples used for ELISA tests included 20 samples from healthy individuals, 10 samples from individuals with premalignant lesions, and 50 samples from CRC patients at stages I–IV ( ; Table S1 ). Exosome Isolation and Characterization Plasma sEVs from stage II CRC patients with recurrent and nonrecurrent CRC were isolated using the qEV original 70 nm Columns (Izon), following manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 500 μL of plasma was loaded into the isolation columns, and sEVs were collected in fractions 1–4 of 500 μL of PBS 1× each after elution of the death column volume. The protein concentration of fractions containing sEVs was measured by microBCA (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For isolation, 2 separate columns were employed, one for the 5 samples from recurrent CRC and another for the 5 samples from nonrecurrent CRC patients. Then, the most concentrated fractions (fraction 4 for all samples) were analyzed by electron transmission microscopy (TEM) using a FEI Tecnai 12 electron microscope and NTA (Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis) using a NanoSight NS300 (Malvern Panalytical) to verify the quality of purified exosomes, as previously described. , , sEVs were stored at −80 °C until use. Cell Lines Two isogenic cell models of human CRC, KM12, and SW systems were used. The KM12 model is composed of the poorly metastatic KM12C cell line and the two highly metastatic cell lines, KM12SM (metastatic to liver) and KM12L4a (metastatic to liver and lungs). The SW model is composed of the poorly metastatic SW480 cell line and the metastatic lymph node SW620 cell line. KM12 cells were obtained from I. Fidler’s laboratory (MD Anderson Cancer Center), whereas SW cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection cell repository. − All cell lines were grown at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Lonza, Basel) supplemented with 1× l -glutamine (Lonza), 1× penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza), and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Sigma-Aldrich). Protein Extraction and Quantification Protein extraction from FFPE tissue is inherently challenging due to formalin-induced cross-linking and protein modifications, which can limit absolute protein recovery compared to fresh or frozen samples. Therefore, the FFPE extraction workflow employed here was previously optimized. Briefly, FFPE tissues were incubated twice with 500 μL of heptane (Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 h at room temperature (RT) and 700 rpm, rehydrated with 25 μL of 100% methanol, and centrifuged at 15,000 g for 5 min to collect tissues and remove paraffin. Then, deparaffinized tissues were lysed with 400 μL of lysis buffer (RIPA buffer, Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 1× protease and phosphatase inhibitors (MedChemExpress) by mechanical disaggregation using the TissueLyser II (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) (2 cycles of 30 s at 30 Hz). Then, tissues were incubated at 700 rpm at 100 °C for 20 min and at 80 °C for 2 h to remove paraffin traces and reverse cross-linking. After centrifugation at 10,000 g and 4 °C for 10 min, protein extracts (supernatants) were transferred to a new tube and stored at −80 °C until use. For the WB analysis of OCT-embedded paired tumoral and nontumoral tissue samples, tissues were cut from the OCT blocks and washed twice with 500 μL of PBS 1× followed by centrifugation at 10,000 g for 10 min and 4 °C. Then, tissues were lysed with RIPA buffer supplemented with 1× protease and phosphatase inhibitors using the TissueLyser II (Qiagen) (2 cycles of 30 s at 30 Hz). After centrifugation at 10,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C, supernatants (protein extracts) were collected and stored at −80 °C until use. For WB analysis of CRC cells, cells were grown until 90% confluency, detached using 4 mM EDTA PBS 1×, and collected by centrifugation at 1200 rpm and RT for 5 min. Cell pellets were then resuspended in 500 μL of RIPA buffer supplemented with 1× protease and phosphatase inhibitors and lysed using 25 gauge syringes. Finally, samples were centrifuged at 10,000 g and 4 °C for 10 min, and protein extracts were collected in new tubes to be stored at −80 °C until used. The protein concentration of tissue samples and cell extracts was determined by the tryptophan quantification method. sEVs protein concentration was determined by microBCA. , Proteomics Analysis

90% confluency, detached using 4 mM EDTA PBS 1×, and collected by centrifugation at 1200 rpm and RT for 5 min. Cell pellets were then resuspended in 500 μL of RIPA buffer supplemented with 1× protease and phosphatase inhibitors and lysed using 25 gauge syringes. Finally, samples were centrifuged at 10,000 g and 4 °C for 10 min, and protein extracts were collected in new tubes to be stored at −80 °C until used. The protein concentration of tissue samples and cell extracts was determined by the tryptophan quantification method. sEVs protein concentration was determined by microBCA. , Proteomics Analysis and TMT Labeling Protein extracts from tissue samples and sEVs isolated from paired plasma samples were analyzed by TMT (tandem mass tags) liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS). Tissue and sEVs samples from stage II CRC patients with recurrent ( n = 5) and nonrecurrent ( n = 5) disease were analyzed separately, using two independent 10-plex TMT kits. For tissue samples, 10 μg of each protein extract in 100 μL of RIPA buffer was used and reduced with 10 mM tris­(2-carboxyethyl)­phosphine (TCEP, Sigma-Aldrich) and alkylated with 40 mM chloroacetamide (Sigma-Aldrich) prior digestion, as previously described. , , For sEVs samples, 10 μg of each sample was lysed with 250 μL of RIPA buffer using 25 gauge syringes. In addition, after lysis, sEVs samples were incubated 5 times at 95 °C for 5 min and in ice for 5 min to ensure complete lysis of sEVs. Then, samples were reduced and alkylated prior to digestion, as described above. Digestion was performed on SP3 magnetic beads (50% hydrophilic beads–50% hydrophobic beads, GE Healthcare) after protein incubation with the beads and 50% acetonitrile (ACN) for 35 min at RT and in rotation. Digestion was performed with 0.4 μg of porcine trypsin (1:20, Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 100 μL of 200 mM HEPES pH 8.0 overnight (O/N) and at 37 °C and 1000 rpm. After digestion, samples were separately labeled with 0.4 mg of each TMT reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Briefly, 0.8 mg of each TMT reagent that covalently labels the primary amines of Lys and the N-termini of trypsin-digested peptides were resuspended in 41 μL of 100% ACN. Samples were first incubated with 10 μL of the corresponding TMT reagent for 30 min at 600 rpm and RT, followed by a second incubation with 10 μL of the same reagent for 30 min at 600 rpm and RT. After labeling, the reaction was quenched with 10 μL of 1 M glycine incubated for 30 min at 600 rpm and RT. Then, the 10 different samples per TMT experiment were pooled together and dried under vacuum, and labeled peptides were separated according to their hydrophobicity using a High pH Reversed-Phase Peptide Fractionation Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), as previously described. After fractionation, peptides were divided into 12 fractions of 300 μL each in a triethylamine-ACN gradient (2.5–100% ACN). Peptide fractions were mixed in six fractions, dried under vacuum, and stored at −80 °C until LC–MS/MS analysis using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to the FAIMS Pro Due Interface (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Remarkably, although absolute protein yield from FFPE samples may be reduced in comparison to other proteomics studies, TMT-based labeling would enable robust relative quantification, as all samples within each experiment were processed, labeled, pooled, and analyzed in parallel. Therefore, differences in extraction efficiency were expected to primarily affect proteome coverage rather than introduce systematic bias in relative protein quantification in proteomics analyses. LC–MS/MS Analysis The six peptide fractions of the 2 TMT experiments were resuspended in 10 μL of 0.1% formic acid (FA). For the tissue samples, 4 μL of each fraction was injected per run, whereas for the sEVs samples, 6 μL of each fraction was injected per run. Peptide separation was carried out on the Vanquish Neo UHPLC System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) as previously described. Briefly, peptide samples were loaded into a precolumn PepMap 100 C18 3 μm, 75 μm × 2 cm Nanoviper Trap 1200BA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and eluted in an Easy-Spray PepMap RSLC C18 2 μm, 75 μm × 50 cm (Thermo Fisher Scientific) heated at 50 °C. The mobile phase flow rate was 300 nL/min, with buffer A (0.1% FA in H 2 Omq) and buffer B (0.1% FA in 80% ACN) used for elution. A 2 h gradient was set as follows: 0–2% buffer B for 4 min, 2% buffer B for 2 min, 2–42% buffer B for 100 min, 42–72% buffer B for 14 min, 72–95% buffer B for 5 min, and 95% buffer B for 10 min. For ionization, 1900 V of liquid junction voltage and 280 °C capillary temperature were used. The full scan method employed a m / z 350–1400 mass selection, an Orbitrap resolution of 60,000

was 300 nL/min, with buffer A (0.1% FA in H 2 Omq) and buffer B (0.1% FA in 80% ACN) used for elution. A 2 h gradient was set as follows: 0–2% buffer B for 4 min, 2% buffer B for 2 min, 2–42% buffer B for 100 min, 42–72% buffer B for 14 min, 72–95% buffer B for 5 min, and 95% buffer B for 10 min. For ionization, 1900 V of liquid junction voltage and 280 °C capillary temperature were used. The full scan method employed a m / z 350–1400 mass selection, an Orbitrap resolution of 60,000 (at m / z 200), an automatic gain control (AGC) value of 300%, and a maximum injection time (IT) of 25 ms. After the survey scan, the 12 most intense precursor ions were selected for MS/MS fragmentation. Fragmentation was performed with a normalized collision energy of 34, and MS/MS scans were acquired with a 100 m / z first mass, an AGC target of 100%, a resolution of 15,000 (at m / z 200), an intensity threshold of 2 × 10 4 , an isolation window of 0.7 m / z units, a maximum IT of 22 ms, and TurboTMT enabled. Charge state screening was enabled to reject unassigned, singly charged, and greater than or equal to seven protonated ions. A dynamic exclusion time of 30 s was used to discriminate against previously selected ions. For FAIMS, a gas flow of 4.7 L/min and CVs = −45 V and −60 V was used. MS Data Analysis MS data were analyzed with MaxQuant (version 1.6.6.0) using standardized workflows. Mass spectra *.raw files were searched against Uniprot UP000005640_9606.fasta Homo sapiens (human) 2019 database (20962 protein entries) using the Reporter ion MS2 type. TMT10 was specified as variable modification on lysine and peptide N termini, and reporter ion intensities were bias-corrected for the overlapping isotope contributions from the TMT tags according to manufacturer’s certificate. Precursor and reporter mass tolerance were set to 4.5 ppm and 0.003 Da, respectively, allowing 2 missed cleavages. Carbamidomethylation of cysteines was set as a fixed modification, and methionine oxidation and acetylation N-terminal were set as variable modifications. Unique and Razor peptides were considered for quantification, with a minimal peptide length of 7 amino acids and a maximal peptide mass of 4600 Da. Identified peptides were filtered by their precursor intensity fraction (PIF) with a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.01. The protein sequence coverage was estimated for specific proteins by the percentage of matching amino acids from the identified peptides having a confidence greater than or equal to 95% divided by the total number of amino acids in the sequence. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the data set identifier PXD060933. The statistical and differential expression analysis for the identification of dysregulated proteins associated with CRC recurrency was performed with R Studio (version 4.1.1) using the packages “dplyr”, “tidyverse”, “limma”, “edgeR”, “ggplot2”, and “rstatix”. A moderated t -statistics analysis was performed after data filtering (proteins identified in at least 60% of samples were considered for the analysis), and missing values were imputation by random draws from a Gaussian, using the “imputeLCMD” R package. Proteins identified with a fold change (expression ratio) ≥ 1.5 or ≤ 0.67 (log 2 -transformed expression ratios ≥ 0.58 or ≤ −0.58, respectively) and p -value ≤ 0.05 were selected as statistically significant dysregulated proteins. SDS-PAGE and Western Blot Protein expression was assessed using Coomassie blue staining, silver staining, and Western blot (WB) analysis. For WB, protein extracts were separated on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel, transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes, and treated with primary and secondary antibodies following standard protocols in blocking buffer (0.1% Tween PBS 1× containing 3% skim milk) at the corresponding dilutions ( Table S2 ). The signal was developed using the ECL Pico Plus chemiluminescent substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and captured with the Amersham ImageQuant 800 system (Cytiva). Protein band intensities were quantified using ImageJ software. Transient Silencing of CDCA2 JetPrime transfection reagent (PolyPlus) was employed to transfect CRC cell lines with control siRNA (SIC001, Sigma-Aldrich) and CDCA2 siRNA (EHU045441, Sigma-Aldrich) following previously established protocols. , 48 h after transfection, cells were analyzed by quantitative PCR (qPCR). Alternatively, 24 h after transfection cells were used for proliferation, adhesion, or wound-healing loss-of-function assays. , All in vitro assays were performed in duplicate (biological replicates). RNA Extraction and qPCR CRC cell lines were grown until 90% confluency, harvested with trypsin–EDTA, and centrifuged at 1200 rpm at RT for 5 min. Supernatants were removed, and the pellets were used to isolate the RNA. For RNA extraction, cell pellets were incubated in 500 μL of NZYol (NZYTech) for 5 min at RT. Then, 100 μL of chloroform was added to each sample,

after transfection, cells were analyzed by quantitative PCR (qPCR). Alternatively, 24 h after transfection cells were used for proliferation, adhesion, or wound-healing loss-of-function assays. , All in vitro assays were performed in duplicate (biological replicates). RNA Extraction and qPCR CRC cell lines were grown until 90% confluency, harvested with trypsin–EDTA, and centrifuged at 1200 rpm at RT for 5 min. Supernatants were removed, and the pellets were used to isolate the RNA. For RNA extraction, cell pellets were incubated in 500 μL of NZYol (NZYTech) for 5 min at RT. Then, 100 μL of chloroform was added to each sample, incubated again for 3 min at RT after mixing, and centrifuged for 15 min at 12,000 g and 4 °C. After centrifugation, supernatants containing RNA were transferred to new tubes and mixed with 70% ethanol. RNA purification was subsequently performed with the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen), following manufacturer’s indications. RNA concentration was measured in a NanoDrop 2000C (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After RNA isolation and purification, cDNA synthesis was performed with the NZY First-Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (NZYTech), using 1 μg of total RNA, according to manufacturer’s protocol. A p -value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results In this work, we aimed to identify dysregulated proteins associated with CRC recurrence. To this end, TMT quantitative proteomics was used to analyze FFPE tissue and plasma samples from CRC stage II patients with and without recurrence during follow-up. After deparaffinization of tissue samples and isolation of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) from paired plasma, tissue, and sEVs protein extracts were analyzed by proteomics. Validation of mass spectrometry results was performed via WB of cell extracts and tissue, ELISA of plasma samples, immunohistochemistry, in silico analysis, and cell-based functional assays. Isolation and Characterization of sEVs from Plasma of CRC Patients Prior to proteomics analysis, the quality of the sEVs isolated by column filtration from plasma of CRC patients, whose paired FFPE tissue was also available, was analyzed by NTA and TEM. By NTA, a multimodal distribution was observed with the presence of heterogeneous sEVs in size, where the predominant sEVs sizes in all samples were smaller than 200 nm, ranging between 50 and 200 nm ( A). Additionally, we confirmed an appropriate isolation of the sEVs by TEM, where the size and morphology of the vesicles were compatible with sEVs ( B). Finally, immunostaining with the specific sEVs marker Alix confirmed the correct isolation of the sEVs derived from the conditioned medium of the cells ( C). For the proteomics characterization of CRC recurrence, paired tissue and plasma samples from 5 stage II CRC patients with recurrence and 5 stage II CRC patients without recurrence during follow-up were used ( ). Two independent TMT experiments were conducted: one for the proteome analysis of FFPE tissue samples and another for the proteome analysis of paired plasma sEVs. Both experiments were performed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 instrument equipped with a FAIMS Pro Duo interface. MaxQuant and R software were utilized for protein identification, quantification, and dysregulation analysis. After sample loading normalization of sEVs and tissue protein intensities was performed with R Studio to equalize the median total signal intensity per channel ( Figure S1A ), a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed to analyze sample clustering ( Figure S1B ). A high degree of interindividual biological variability was observed among stage II CRC patients, both in recurrent and nonrecurrent cases. Despite the observed differences among samples mainly attributed to interindividual variability, 3 out of 5 recurrent tissue samples clustered separately from nonrecurrent samples. Moreover, all recurrent sEVs samples formed a distinct cluster from nonrecurrent sEVs. Thus, all samples were used for the subsequent differential expression analysis with the objective to identify proteins associated with the recurrence state in CRC patients, regardless of interindividual heterogeneity. In total, 574 and 343 proteins were identified and quantified in tissue samples and sEVs from stage II CRC patients, respectively ( Tables S3 and S4 ). Statistical analysis was subsequently conducted to identify dysregulated proteins associated with CRC recurrence. Proteins with log 2 expression ratios ≥ 0.58 (upregulated) or ≤ −0.58 (downregulated), along with a moderated p -value ≤ 0.05, were considered statistically significantly dysregulated. For FFPE tissue samples, 59 proteins were identified as dysregulated, with 31 proteins showing downregulation and 28 proteins upregulation ( A), whereas for sEVs samples, a total of 25 proteins were identified as dysregulated, with 6 downregulated and 10 upregulated ( A; Tables S3 and S4 ), with no proteins in common in both proteomics analyses. Subsequently, Gene Ontology (GO) and STRING analyses were performed using the dysregulated proteins from each TMT experiment. GO analysis of FFPE tissue-dysregulated proteins revealed among the three more enriched components cytosolic, cytoplasmic, and nuclear proteins and proteins associated with cell signaling and translation processes ( B). Although the GO term “extracellular exosome” was also enriched in FFPE samples in the fourth position, this would likely reflect the broad annotation of proteins previously detected in exosomes rather than the physical presence or isolation of extracellular vesicles from FFPE tissues. STRING analysis of these proteins showed a high variety of pathways, including proteins implicated in translation, mRNA processing, and oxidation–reduction processes ( C). In contrast, for sEVs proteins, the top three enriched components were the extracellular region, extracellular space, and extracellular exosomes in concordance with the expected vesicular origin of these samples ( B). Additionally, these sEVs dysregulated proteins were related to the immune response, and a single cluster associated with complement activation was obtained ( B,C). Validation of Dysregulated Proteins Next, 7 proteins were selected for subsequent validation by orthogonal techniques: WB, in silico analyses, and immunohistochemistry. The selection criteria of candidate proteins were based on the highest ratio of expression, antibody availability, and novelty in their association with cancer and, more specifically, CRC and CRC recurrence ( ). Therefore, in total, five proteins from the FFPE tissue TMT and two from the sEVs TMT were analyzed to determine if they were at least dysregulated in tumoral tissue in comparison to paired healthy tissue from the same CRC patients. To address this issue and validate proteomics data, paired healthy and tumoral tissue extracts from 7 CRC patients’ OCT-embedded biopsies from stage I to IV were first analyzed by WB. OCT-tissues from CRC patients at different stages of the disease were used due to (i) unavailability of tissue samples from CRC recurrence cases and (ii) because FFPE tissue is not recommended for WB due to extensive protein cross-linking caused by formalin fixation, which masks epitopes and alters protein structure, extensively limiting antibody binding efficiency. Among these proteins, MANF showed the most significant change in expression between healthy and tumoral tissues regardless of the stage of the disease, with its upregulation consistent with the proteomics data ( A,B). In addition, the dysregulation observed for PPIA, TLN1, NAP1L1, CDCA2, and PI4KA in tumoral tissue in comparison to paired nontumoral tissue was in concordance with the dysregulation observed by proteomics ( A,B). Furthermore, the dysregulation of PPIA was mainly observed at early stages I–II of the disease, whereas NAP1L1 was downregulated especially at advanced III–IV CRC stages and TLN1 upregulated at early and advanced stages of the disease ( B). In contrast, slight differences were observed for PI4KA and CDCA2, at early and advanced CRC stages ( A,B). Interestingly, TALDO1 showed higher expression in tumoral tissues, at both early and advanced stages, despite having been previously described by proteomics as downregulated in recurrent CRC ( A,B). Additionally, WB validation was performed by using cellular extracts from isogenic KM12 and SW cell models of CRC metastasis to explore potential links between protein expression and CRC progression and metastasis. Importantly, for TLN1 and NAP1L1, two immunoreactive bands were detected in tissue protein extracts, which likely reflect the presence of protein isoforms, post-translational modifications, or partial proteolytic processing commonly observed in complex tissue lysates. In contrast, metastatic CRC cell lines displayed a single predominant band, which was consistent with a more homogeneous protein population. All selected proteins demonstrated consistent associations with metastasis and recurrence, with CDCA2 showing particularly notable changes in the expression in metastatic cell models (

First, distinct survival profiles were observed at the mRNA level using the COAD data set of the TCGA for each protein, reflecting diverse biological roles in CRC ( A). In this sense, a significant association of MANF ( p -value = 0.027) and CDCA2 ( p -value = 0.0075) with better overall survival and TALDO1 ( p -value = 0.03) with poorer patients’ survival was determined ( A), with no significant association of NAP1L1 with patient’s survival ( p -value = 0.066). Next, immunohistochemical analysis using a stage II CRC-specific TMA revealed distinct expression patterns for MANF, CDCA2, NAP1L1, and TALDO1 across CRC tissue samples ( B). MANF exhibited a predominantly cytoplasmic staining with perinuclear enhancement, consistent with its role in endoplasmic reticulum stress response. , CDCA2 showed strong nuclear positivity in proliferating epithelial cells, reflecting its function in chromatin condensation and cell cycle progression. NAP1L1 displayed both nuclear and cytoplasmic localization, indicative of its dual role in nucleosome assembly and transcriptional regulation. TALDO1 staining was cytoplasmic and variable in intensity, consistent with its involvement in the pentose phosphate pathway. Together, these patterns demonstrate the heterogeneous yet widespread expression of all four proteins in malignant epithelial cells. Moreover, Kaplan–Meier analysis of the IHC results showed significant differences for CDCA2 and NAP1L1 ( C), with an association of CDCA2 and NAP1L1 with better overall survival. Additionally, a trend was observed whereby patients with high CDCA2 protein expression exhibited shorter recurrence-free survival after a first CRC recurrence compared to those with low expression, suggesting a potential association with increased recurrence risk, as observed by proteomics. Collectively, these findings confirmed MANF, CDCA2, NAP1L1, and TALDO1 as prognostically relevant biomarkers in CRC at either the mRNA or protein level, highlighting potential implications at the functional level and as potential informative biomarkers for patient risk stratification and recurrence monitoring in CRC. CDCA2 Silencing Alters Tumorigenic Properties of CRC Cells Next, we focused on determining the potential association of the validated proteins to CRC progression and metastasis in vitro by means of loss-of-function cell-based assays ( ). CDCA2 -due to its higher differential expression observed in the metastatic KM12SM and SW620 CRC cells in comparison with their isogenic poorly metastatic counterparts KM12C and SW480 CRC cells by WB ( )- was selected for subsequent functional analysis. CDCA2 transient depletion was confirmed by qPCR at the mRNA level in the isogenic cell models of CRC metastasis (KM12 and the pair SW480/SW620) prior to subsequent loss-of-function cell-based in vitro analysis ( A). Next, the impact of CDCA2 transient depletion on cell adhesion, proliferation, and migration was analyzed ( B,C). Cell adhesion was significantly increased upon CDCA2 knockdown in most cell lines, particularly in the highly metastatic KM12SM and KM12L4a cells, suggesting that reduced CDCA2 levels promote stronger cell–matrix interactions that may facilitate subsequent invasion. Similarly, cell proliferation was significantly elevated upon CDCA2 depletion. In contrast, cell motility, assessed by wound-healing assays, was modestly altered with no consistent increase in migration speed, indicating that CDCA2 loss primarily affects adhesive and proliferative behaviors rather than migration. Collectively, our findings reveal that CDCA2 silencing enhances adhesion and proliferation, hallmarks of aggressive cancer phenotypes. Importantly, these results align with the clinical Kaplan–Meier analysis, where low CDCA2 expression correlates with worse patient survival. MANF Protein Levels in Plasma Demonstrate an Association of MANF with CRC Recurrence Finally, we focused the study on determining the potential of the identified proteins as plasma biomarkers of CRC and/or CRC recurrence. MANF was prioritized for further analysis since it displayed the most significant expression alterations in CRC tumor tissue, suggesting that its overexpression could promote its release into the bloodstream. Then, MANF protein levels were quantified in plasma by ELISA using samples from healthy individuals ( n = 20), patients with premalignant lesions (low- and high-grade colorectal adenomas, n = 10), and CRC patients with ( n = 22) and without recurrence ( n = 28) at the different stages of the disease. Interestingly, plasma MANF levels increased from healthy individuals (365.02 pg/mL) to patients with premalignant lesions (793.29 pg/mL) and decreased slightly in CRC cases (621.85 pg/mL) ( A). This pattern allowed significant discrimination between healthy and disease groups, highlighting MANF’s potential as an early circulating biomarker. Furthermore, the potential of MANF as a CRC plasma biomarker was evaluated by means of the ROC curves. Plasma MANF levels showed a high capacity to discriminate healthy individuals from CRC patients and from individuals with premalignant lesions, with a diagnostic capacity (area under the curve, AUC) of 64.85% and 81%, respectively, and specificities higher than 70% in both cases ( B). In contrast, MANF did not possess the capacity to discriminate CRC patients from individuals with premalignant lesions. Additionally, a remarkable trend in MANF plasma concentration was observed between recurrent (494.88 pg/mL) and nonrecurrent CRC patients’ samples (721.62 pg/mL), with a diagnostic capacity of 63.47% and a sensitivity of 77.27%, highlighting a potential role as biomarker of nonrecurrence in plasma of CRC patients ( A,B), consistent across disease stages II–IV. Indeed, the ROC curve analysis differentiating nonrecurrent and recurrent CRC patients yielded an AUC of 63% (sensitivity 77%, specificity 50%). Consistent with the tissue-based survival analysis ( ), where high MANF expression in tumor samples was associated with improved overall survival, plasma measurements revealed that elevated circulating MANF levels correlate with the absence of recurrence and a better clinical outcome in CRC patients. MANF concentrations were highest in individuals with premalignant lesions and declined progressively in advanced and recurrent disease, suggesting that the systemic abundance of MANF reflects preserved cellular stress-control capacity and lower CRC progression and aggressiveness. Discussion Proteomic analysis has become a powerful tool for identifying biomarkers associated with cancer formation, progression, and metastasis, while recurrence analyses are not so extended. Here, our study highlights how the proteomic profiling of FFPE tissues and sEVs enables the identification of proteins linked to tumor recurrence in stage II CRC patients. FFPE and sEVs serve as complementary sources of analyses. , , , FFPE tissues preserve in situ protein expression, providing a snapshot of the tumor microenvironment, while sEVs circulate systemically and may reflect real-time tumor dynamics. The combined analysis of both sources enhanced here the identification of proteins related to stage II CRC patients. Although the overall proteome depth was limited due to the intrinsic complexity and compromised quality of the samples, FAIMS proved essential to enhance ion selection, reduce chemical noise, and improve proteome coverage, in line with previous reports. Without FAIMS, it was nearly impossible to achieve sufficient proteome depth from such challenging materials, including cross-linked FFPE tissues and low-volume plasma-derived sEVs. Despite these constraints, the use of paired samples from the same patient remains a powerful strategy in oncological biomarker discovery. Analyzing multiple sample types from a single individual allows for the detection of dynamic changes in biomarker expression from plasma sEVs to primary tumors, thereby controlling for interindividual variability and increasing the reliability of results. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the identification of molecular alterations associated with disease progression or treatment response, reinforcing the potential of personalized and recurrence-risk-oriented medicine in CRC. Here, we have focused on reinforcing its role in refining recurrence risk prediction in the CRC. A limitation of this study is the relatively small size of the FFPE cohort used for quantitative proteomics in addition to the intrinsic interindividual heterogeneity of clinically derived paired tissue and plasma samples. This heterogeneity likely contributes to the limited sample clustering observed in the PCA analysis of FFPE tissue proteomes. PCA was indeed used as an exploratory tool rather than a criterion for patient stratification. Importantly, this limitation was mitigated in the study, integrating the parallel analysis of paired FFPE tissue and sEVs isolated from plasma samples, TMT-based quantitative proteomics, validation using independent OCT-embedded frozen tissue and plasma samples, and functional cell-based assays. The consistent identification of specific protein alterations across independent biological CRC samples and orthogonal experimental approaches supported the biological relevance and robustness

PCA was indeed used as an exploratory tool rather than a criterion for patient stratification. Importantly, this limitation was mitigated in the study, integrating the parallel analysis of paired FFPE tissue and sEVs isolated from plasma samples, TMT-based quantitative proteomics, validation using independent OCT-embedded frozen tissue and plasma samples, and functional cell-based assays. The consistent identification of specific protein alterations across independent biological CRC samples and orthogonal experimental approaches supported the biological relevance and robustness of the identified candidates, despite the inherent observed interindividual heterogeneity of the discovery cohort. One of the goals of the study was the identification of potential markers related to CRC recurrence. In this sense, two proteins emerged as interesting proteins associated with recurrence and progression in the CRC: CDCA2 and MANF. CDCA2 (Cell Division Cycle Associated 2) was significantly overexpressed in CRC tissues and plays a key role in tumor progression. , , Our study revealed that transient depletion of CDCA2 enhanced proliferation and adhesion, with only a minor effect on migration in CRC cells, supporting its potential involvement in CRC progression and metastasis. These functional findings were consistent with survival analyses from both TCGA data and immunohistochemistry, which showed that low CDCA2 expression correlated to poorer overall survival at the time of diagnosis. Interestingly, high CDCA2 expression was later associated with poorer recurrence-free survival when evaluating its levels at a second recurrence, in agreement with our proteomics data and suggesting changes in the functional role of CDCA2 during tumor evolution. This apparently paradoxical observationwhere a proliferation-associated gene corresponds to better prognosis at diagnosis but worse outcome at recurrencemay indicate that CDCA2 expression initially reflects a more differentiated and phenotypically stable tumor state, whereas its downregulation could favor dedifferentiation and acquisition of a more aggressive phenotype. However, at the recurrence stage, sustained CDCA2 activity might also represent a compensatory cellular mechanism aimed at maintaining proliferative control in an otherwise unstable tumor environment. Importantly, our findings align with previous research demonstrating that CDCA2 facilitates tumor growth by modulating cell cycle regulators and activating the AKT/CCND1 pathway, while gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) confirmed a positive association between CDCA2 expression and cell cycle phase transition genes, particularly those driving the G1-S phase transition. Altogether, these findings support a model in which CDCA2 contributes to CRC progression by promoting cell cycle regulation, while its loss may facilitate tumor dedifferentiation and increased aggressiveness. Regarding MANF, it is a protein primarily recognized for its neuroprotective properties, particularly in the context of neurodegenerative diseases. , Recent studies have begun to explore its role in cancer biology. , − Here, besides the interesting role as a CRC diagnostic biomarker, we have demonstrated a remarkable trend of MANF toward no recurrence of CRC patients in plasma, suggesting MANF as a protective biomarker, with higher plasma levels correlating with a lower recurrence risk in CRC patients but with a moderate discriminative power in predicting disease recurrence by ROC curve analyses. Moreover, TCGA data analysis from the COAD data set supports this observation, revealing an inverse relationship between MANF expression and tumor aggressiveness. Given MANF’s function in maintaining endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and proteostasis homeostasis, , higher plasma levels may denote a protective, antitumorigenic environment capable of limiting chronic ER stress and inflammation during carcinogenesis. Conversely, MANF downregulation in plasma would likely indicate loss of adaptive homeostatic responses, favoring tumor progression, recurrence, and poorer survival. Together, these findings support a context-dependent prognostic role for MANF in CRCits elevated expression in circulation associates with reduced recurrence risk and prolonged patient survival, reinforcing its role as a protective modulator of tumor stress responses. While cohort size and interindividual heterogeneity in the TMT-quantitative proteomic analyses may contribute to variability in effect size, the consistent observation of opposite MANF regulation across tissue and plasma, supported by independent validation and in silico analyses, argues against a technical or stochastic explanation. In contrast, elevated protein levels of MANF in tissues are associated with prolonged patient survival but a higher risk of recurrence in our cohort. Accordingly, MANF’s cytoprotective and anti-inflammatory functions could contribute to improved patient outcomes. Therefore, the integration of MANF together with existing prognostic models may refine CRC risk stratification, helping to identify patients who could benefit from less aggressive treatment approaches while maintaining favorable survival rates. Finally, while this study provides compelling evidence for the prognostic potential of CDCA2 and MANF, further validation in larger, independent, and longitudinal cohorts will be required to confirm their clinical utility. Moreover, the integration of MANF with multiomic markers, using multilevel platforms for their analyses, , should allow to develop more robust patient stratification tools refining prognostic models to guide personalized follow-up and therapeutic strategies in CRC.
